candidates.heading: Theorem 1.1 (Unique Games Theorem).
candidates.statement: For every fixed ε, δ ∈ (0, 1/2), there are an integer s ≥ 1 and a deterministic polynomial-time reduction from 3SAT to explicit unweighted Unique Games instances Gφ over K = Fs 2 such that φ satisfiable =⇒ val(Gφ) ≥ 1 − ε, φ unsatisfiable =⇒ val(Gφ) ≤ δ. candidates.name: Raghavendra’s consequence
candidates.heading: Corollary 8.1 (Raghavendra’s consequence).
candidates.statement: Let J be a fixed Λ-instance with A = OPT(J) < B = SDPR(J). For every fixed 0 < η < (B − A)/2, it is NP-hard to distinguish Λ-instances I satisfying OPT(I) ≥ B − η from those satisfying OPT(I) ≤ A + η.

candidates.label: Corollary 8.2
candidates.name: Ordering-CSP consequence
candidates.heading: Corollary 8.2 (Ordering-CSP consequence).
candidates.statement: Fix k ≥ 2 and ∅ ̸= Π ⊊ Sk, and put ρΠ = |Π|/k!. For every fixed 0 < ε < (1 − ρΠ)/2, it is NP-hard to distinguish finite weighted Π-ordering-CSP instances I satisfying OPTΠ(I) ≥ 1 − ε from those satisfying OPTΠ(I) ≤ ρΠ + ε. Consequently, approximation at every fixed ratio r ∈ (ρΠ, 1] is NP-hard. Together with the random- ordering guarantee, this gives the optimal threshold ρΠ.

candidates.label: Corollary 8.3
candidates.name: Cut, deletion, and clustering hardness
candidates.heading: Corollary 8.3 (Cut, deletion, and clustering hardness).
candidates.statement: For every fixed real constant C > 1, it is NP-hard to approximate each of the four minimization problems above within factor C. For Sparsest Cut, this is hardness of the search task under polynomial-time Cook reductions: the algorithm must output a cutset, not only an estimate of the optimum. Consequently, unless P = NP, none of these problems admits a deterministic polynomial-time approximation with any fixed constant factor.

candidates.statement: Fix k ≥ 2 and ∅ ̸= Π ⊊ Sk, put ρΠ = |Π|/k!, and fix 0 < δ < (1 − ρΠ)/2. There are integers q, H ≥ 1 and positive rationals ζ, ν < 1, depending only on k, Π, δ, with the following property for every fixed integer R ≥ 1. Let Φ = (A, B, E) be a nonempty explicit unweighted simple bipartite Unique Games instance over [R], oriented from A to B, whose common left degree h satisfies h ≥ H and q | h. There is a deterministic transformation, polynomial in the explicit size of Φ for fixed R, producing an explicit list of Π-ordering constraints on distinct variables within each constraint, with nonnegative rational weights, each encoded by a binary numerator and a positive binary denominator, summing to one. If some labeling strongly satisfies at least (1 − ζ)|A| left vertices, then OPTΠ(I) ≥ 1 − δ. If val(Φ) ≤ ν, then OPTΠ(I) ≤ ρΠ + δ. The constants q, H, ζ, ν are independent of both R and h.

Every test or numerical digit query terminates, returns its defined value, and restores the cursor and catalyst. Its result is independent of incoming catalyst and scratch contents. Structural port and order choices are independent of a higher numerical request. 2. Terminal motions give the specified endpoints. Their excursions restore the cursor. Capped correction motions are partial paired maps with bounded inverse ports and safe behavior on invalid ports. Incoming score ranks compute the stipulated zero-padded ranks. 3. For a root numerical request at clock t, all records retained by the call and its descendants have total length O(Mtop + t + 1), and every descendant clock is O(Mtop + t + 1); the shared facilities use O(B + Mtop + t + 1) space. In particular an actual top request with t = O(B) uses total deterministic O(B) space. These implementations use no estimator oracle and retain no second vertex address across recursive graph operations.

There is a single positional Max strategy winning from every vertex of Ump(H), and a single positional Min strategy forcing strictly negative liminf mean payoff from every vertex outside it. Both guarantees hold against every history-dependent opposing strategy.

candidates.label: Theorem 3.2
candidates.heading: Theorem 3.2.
candidates.statement: In every finite arena, each vertex is winning for exactly one of Max and Min. From each vertex winning for Max, there is a conjunction-winning strategy satisfying (2).

candidates.label: Theorem 4.1
candidates.name: Bounded-dominion guarantee
candidates.heading: Theorem 4.1 (Bounded-dominion guarantee).
candidates.statement: For every subarena H of the original game and every b ∈ {0, . . . , n}2, the procedure Solve(H, b) terminates and returns a partition satisfying (4) for both players.

candidates.label: Proposition 5.1
candidates.name: Cost of the reduction
candidates.heading: Proposition 5.1 (Cost of the reduction).
candidates.statement: For an arena with n ≥ 1 vertices and complete binary input length L, the call Solve(G, (n, n)) makes 2O((log2(n+2))2) calls to the ordinary mean-payoff winning-set subroutine. Each such call has an explicit input of length (L + 2)O(1). Apart from those subroutine calls, the computation takes 2O((log2(n+2))2) (L + 2)O(1) bit operations. All constants are absolute.

manuscripts.title: Deterministic quasipolynomial-time mean-payoff games

candidates.label: Theorem 1.1
candidates.heading: Theorem 1.1.
candidates.statement: A uniform deterministic algorithm returns exactly the set U =   v ∈ V : ∃ Max strategy σ ∀ Min strategies τ, MPw(πv,σ,τ ) ≥ 0 for every game specified above. For an absolute constant C > 0, the complete computation uses at most 2C(log2(L+2))2 bit operations in a standard model polynomially equivalent to a uniform deterministic Turing machine. The bound includes preprocessing, exact arithmetic, recursion, and output of the entire set U.

candidates.label: Proposition 2.2
candidates.name: Winning partition from the wide box
candidates.heading: Proposition 2.2 (Winning partition from the wide box).
candidates.statement: Let h be the box solution in [0, D0]V . Then Vlo = {i : hi ≤ nW}, Vhi = {i : hi ≥ D0 − nW} partition V . There is a positional Max strategy under which every play starting in Vhi has original mean payoff at least zero. There is a positional Min strategy under which every play starting in Vlo has original upper limiting average at most −1/n. Both assertions allow arbitrary history-dependent opposition.

candidates.label: Theorem 2.4
candidates.name: Simultaneous labelling
candidates.heading: Theorem 2.4 (Simultaneous labelling).
candidates.statement: For every input in Equation (2.8), the procedure Label(A, D, a, b) of Section 4 terminates and returns a vector in {+, −}V . It assigns + to every index claimed by any Max witness and − to every index claimed by any Min witness.

candidates.label: Corollary 7.1
candidates.name: Full game solution
candidates.heading: Corollary 7.1 (Full game solution).
candidates.statement: A uniform deterministic algorithm returns the exact value valw(v) as a reduced rational for every v ∈ V and one positional strategy σ⋆ for Max and one positional strategy τ⋆ for Min such that, simultaneously for every v ∈ V and every pair of history-dependent strategies σ, τ, MPw(πv,σ⋆,τ ) ≥ valw(v), MPw(πv,σ,τ⋆ ) ≤ valw(v). The complete computation takes 2O((log2(L+2))2) bit operations.

candidates.label: Corollary 7.2
candidates.name: Randomized full game solution
candidates.heading: Corollary 7.2 (Randomized full game solution).
candidates.statement: For the game model of Theorem 1.1, a uniform randomized algorithm returns all exact values and both globally optimal positional strategies specified in Corollary 7.1 with probability at least 7/8 for the entire output. Its running time is 2O((log2(L+2))2) bit operations on every random tape.

candidates.label: Corollary 8.1
candidates.name: Fixed and minimum energy credits
candidates.heading: Corollary 8.1 (Fixed and minimum energy credits).
candidates.statement: Uniform deterministic algorithms have the following guarantees. 1. Given v and a nonnegative binary integer c, decide whether (v, c) is energy-winning. On a positive answer, return a positional Max policy satisfying Equation (8.1) from that start and credit against every history-dependent Min strategy. 2. Given v, return the exact cmin(v), including the possible answer ∞. On a finite answer, return a positional Max policy winning from v at credit cmin(v). The fixed-credit computation takes 2O((log2(Lc+2))2) bit operations, where Lc is the full explicit input length including the start and credit. The minimum-credit computation takes 2O((log2(L+2))2) bit operations for the original game length L. Handling every vertex by separate per-start searches, including a separate policy for every finite answer, has the same form of total bit bound. Each policy may depend on the queried start and credit; it also wins from that same start at every larger credit.

candidates.label: Corollary 9.1
candidates.name: Tropical feasibility and fixed corank
candidates.heading: Corollary 9.1 (Tropical feasibility and fixed corank).
candidates.statement: For explicitly listed m × n matrices A, B and m-dimensional vectors c, d over Q ∪ {−∞}, feasibility of max   ci, max j (Aij + xj) ≤ max   di, max j (Bij + xj) for every row i is decidable deterministically in 2O((log(L+2))2) bit operations, where L is the complete explicit binary input length. Variables range over R ∪ {−∞}; feasibility with all coordinates finite is decidable within the same bound. Equalities between the two displayed maxima are allowed, interpreted as pairs of inequalities. For a homogeneous system (c = d = −∞), one can also compute the maximal finite-coordinate support of a solution, including the empty support. In particular, the same bound decides feasibility of max-atom systems z ≤ max(x, y) + a, with rational constants a and finite real, equivalently rational, variables. For each fixed integer k ≥ 0, a deterministic algorithm with bit bound 2Ok((log(L+2))2) decides whether an explicitly listed m × n matrix over Q ∪ {−∞}, with m ≥ n ≥ 1, has tropical rank at least n − k. Here tropical rank is the largest order of a square submatrix whose permutation sums have a finite, unique maximum. The rank is zero if no such nonempty submatrix exists.

manuscripts.title: Randomized quasipolynomial-time mean-payoff games

candidates.label: Theorem 1.1
candidates.heading: Theorem 1.1.
candidates.statement: There is a uniform randomized algorithm that, for every such game, returns the entire set U = {v ∈ V : there is a Max strategy σ such that for every Min strategy τ, MPw(πv,σ,τ ) ≥ 0} correctly with probability at least 7/8. For an absolute constant C > 0, on every random tape its total cost is at most 2C(log2(L+2))2 bit operations in a standard model polynomially equivalent to a uniform probabilistic Turing machine. The bound includes preprocessing, recursive calls, intermediate arithmetic, and random- bit generation.

candidates.label: Proposition 2.5
candidates.name: Reduction to a box solution
candidates.heading: Proposition 2.5 (Reduction to a box solution).
candidates.statement: Let x solve the constant box [0, B∗], with B∗ = 8nW as in Equation (2.1). Then the original game’s exact zero-threshold winning set is U = {i ∈ V : xi > B∗/2}. A positional Max strategy guarantees original mean payoff at least zero from every vertex of U. Outside U, a positional Min strategy ensures that every consistent play has original upper limiting average at most −1/n, including against arbitrary history-dependent Max strategies.

candidates.label: Proposition 4.5
candidates.heading: Proposition 4.5.
candidates.statement: For every permitted Solve input, the execution and all its subroutine executions terminate on every random tape. The outputs of Solve and Ask are integer vectors in their respective input boxes. The outputs of Orient and OrientPlus have the stated choice and list types, and each listed set has input measure at most 1/2. Moreover: (i) Tightening makes at most 8ns updates and 16ns + 2 calls to Ask. (ii) A chain of main Solve continuations contains at most K = 8s(g + 1) + 1 (4.2) solver invocations. (iii) One Orient trial visits at most g + 1 orientation invocations and returns at most 2g + 2 sets. Consequently OrientPlus returns at most J(2g + 2) sets, counting repetitions.

candidates.label: Proposition 5.1
candidates.name: Orientation
candidates.heading: Proposition 5.1 (Orientation).
candidates.statement: Assume the lower-rank comparison guarantees stated at the beginning of this section. On a fixed permitted input (a, b; B, α, β, k, m) of rank r, let (χ, H) be the output of Orient. For every fixed admissible subsolution y of [a, b] whose core in Equation (5.1) satisfies α(Iy) > ηk, Pr (χ = Y or ∃H ∈ H : α(Sy ∩ H) > ηk) ≥ 1 − 1 16 . (5.2) Separately, for every fixed admissible supersolution z of [a, b] with β(Iz) > ηm, Pr (χ = Z or ∃H ∈ H : β(Sz ∩ H) > ηm) ≥ 1 − 1 16 . (5.3) On every tape, every set in H has µ-measure at most 1/2. Each probability statement remains valid conditional on a pre-call history that fixes its input and qualifying comparison, when the call uses fresh random bits.

candidates.label: Theorem 6.3
candidates.name: Pointwise comparisons for the solver
candidates.heading: Theorem 6.3 (Pointwise comparisons for the solver).
candidates.statement: Let [a, b] be an allowed integer box with positive integer reference width B ≤ B∗, and let the support weights and budgets be positive rationals. For the output p of Solve, each fixed admissible subsolution y and, separately, each fixed admissible supersolution z satisfy Pr(p ≥ y) ≥ 1 − 1 16 , Pr(p ≤ z) ≥ 1 − 1 16 . These are whole-vector inequalities, as in Equation (3.1): a fixed comparison is chosen before the invocation, and its inequality holds at every coordinate on its success event.

candidates.label: Corollary 6.4
candidates.name: Exact recovery of the top box solution
candidates.heading: Corollary 6.4 (Exact recovery of the top box solution).
candidates.statement: Let x be the box solution for [0, B∗]. Let p be the output of Solve on that box with unit support weights, budgets k = m = n, and reference width B∗. Then Pr(p = x) ≥ 7 8 . Hence {i : pi > B∗/2} is the complete winning set with probability at least 7/8.

candidates.label: Theorem 7.1
candidates.heading: Theorem 7.1.
candidates.statement: The algorithm has a uniform implementation in a standard bit-operation model such that, for every input of bit length L and every random tape, the running time is at most 2C(log2(L+2))2 for an absolute constant C > 0. The bound includes preprocessing, every recursive execution, intermediate arithmetic, and random-bit generation.

candidates.label: Corollary 8.1
candidates.name: Certified winning regions and strategies
candidates.heading: Corollary 8.1 (Certified winning regions and strategies).
candidates.statement: There is a randomized algorithm which, on every tape, uses 2O((log2(L+2))2) bit operations and returns either a failure symbol or the exact winning set together with an integer potential and positional strategies for both players. Whenever it returns these objects, the Max strategy wins from every vertex of the winning set and the Min strategy ensures upper limiting average at most −1/n from every other vertex, against arbitrary opposing strategies. It returns these objects with probability at least 7/8. Repeating independent trials until a certificate is accepted terminates almost surely, never returns an incorrect answer, and has expected bit cost 2O((log2(L+2))2).

manuscripts.title: Perfect completeness for 2-to-1 games

candidates.label: Theorem 1.1
candidates.heading: Theorem 1.1.
candidates.statement: For every fixed rational δ ∈ (0, 1) there are an integer q = q(δ) ≥ 2 and a deterministic polynomial-time reduction from 3-SAT to 2-to-1 games with alphabets [2q] and [q] such that: (i) a satisfiable formula produces a game of value 1; (ii) an unsatisfiable formula produces a game of value at most δ. The output contains a nonempty explicit list of unweighted edge occurrences and an explicit table for every projection map. Every table has exactly two preimages for each right answer. The polynomial running-time bound is in the ordinary binary input length; its degree and constants may depend on the fixed δ.

The fraction on the left is the proportion of edges properly colored by χ, or equivalently cut by its partition into k color classes.

candidates.statement: Let NTW(a, b, c) be the Boolean predicate accepting exactly zero, one, or three true inputs. For every fixed 0 < ε < 3/8, it is NP-hard to distinguish a satisfiable instance with constraints NTW(ℓ1, ℓ2, ℓ3) from one in which every assignment satisfies at most a 5/8 + ε fraction of the constraints; each literal ℓi may be a variable or its negation. Consequently, every language in NP has a polynomial-time verifier using O(log n) random bits and three nonadaptive proof-bit queries, with perfect completeness and soundness at most 5/8 + ε, where n is the input length.

If φ is satisfiable, then Ψ is satisfiable. If φ is unsatisfiable, every assignment violates at least a γ0 fraction of the clauses of Ψ. Clause occurrences are explicitly listed, and the binary encoding length of Ψ is polynomial in that of φ.

manuscripts.title: Hardness of finding large independent sets in three-colorable graphs

candidates.label: Theorem 1.1
candidates.heading: Theorem 1.1.

(i) Every individual question marginal is at most B times uniform measure on S. All samplers are polynomially enumerable finite weighted lists with rational probabilities; every positive seed probability is at least inverse-polynomial in the input size. (ii) If the formula is satisfiable, there is an assignment y : S → F2 accepted by every test in every support. manuscripts.title: Unconditional time lower bounds for Weisfeiler–Leman equivalence

candidates.label: Theorem 1.1
candidates.heading: Theorem 1.1.
candidates.statement: There are absolute constants c > 0 and k0 with the following property. For every fixed integer k ≥ k0 and every correct deterministic decider A for k-Weisfeiler–Leman equivalence, there is an integer n0 = n0(A, k) such that TA(n) ≥ nck for every integer n ≥ n0. This holds for multitape Turing machines and for sequential random-access machines with O(log(n + 2))-bit addresses and words, boundedly many memory accesses per instruction, and fixed instructions 1 computable in time polynomial in the word length. The same bound holds if A is required to decide correctly only on pairs of simple connected uncolored graphs of diameter at most two, with TA(n) maximized over that class. It applies both to the joint replacement-multiset convention for k-dimensional refinement and to the separate-multiset convention defined below.

The construction uses the bounded scalar-form data together with the one-coordinate tables, and enumerates Or,shape(m2) blocks without enumerating all full addresses. An arbitrary equal number of additional vertices can be added to the two graphs while preserving the equivalence, connectedness, and diameter bound.

(iv) The one-axis distance and shared-axis comparison gaps of Lemma 3.6 hold with ∆A = (δ1−λ)/4. For every actual and reference joint tuple satisfying the hypotheses of Lemma 3.7, δ1p ≤ zA + 4p2 + λp and, when p ≤ δ1/16, p ≤ 2zA/δ1. A-only slots require no B constraints for these conclusions. The symmetric B assertions hold as well. All constants are independent of N and of the number of later program slots. The field search has only 8c0d0 indeterminates, at most 26 parity determinant factors, and total degree less than M3 o ; in particular it causes no feedback into C0, λ, or d.

candidates.label: Theorem 5.4
candidates.name: Outer representation interface
candidates.heading: Theorem 5.4 (Outer representation interface).
candidates.statement: There are fixed positive constants δraw, ρraw, fixed integers CL, craw, and uniform deterministic algorithms with the following properties for every End-of-Line input of length N. They construct a directed graph of valid extended labels, represented by canonical words Rv ∈ ({0, 1}L )Γ , |Γ| = N poly(ℓN ), L = (ℓN + Cbase)CL , ℓN = ⌈log2(N + 2)⌉, where Cbase may be any sufficiently large fixed integer. (i) Graph and endpoint data. The graph has indegree and outdegree at most one, no self-edges, and no isolated vertices. It has the public distinguished source v∗ and actual successor v+ ∗ in (5.7); their entire words are computable in poly(N) time. Every other endpoint is mapped in poly(N) time to a nonzero solution of the input End-of-Line instance. Every canonical word is computable from its valid label in polynomial time. (ii) Distance and valid-word testing. Distinct canonical words have normalized symbol distance at least δraw. A uniform center test has perfect completeness and uses only a fixed finite list Π of permutation-neighbors, of cardinality q independent of N. For every fixed α > 0 there is a fixed θα > 0 such that rej(W) < θα =⇒ dist(W, Rv) < α for some valid v. 47 Also rej(W) ≤ q dist(W, Rv) for every valid v. (iii) Local proposals and flags. At each requested center, total deterministic routines on Π(k) compute a next or previous proposed symbol and an existence bit. On Rv the bit is independent of the center and equals the actual edge-existence flag. If it is one, the proposed symbols form exactly the canonical neighboring word; if it is zero, the default proposal is Rv itself. (iv) Value-independent uncertainty correction. There is a total local one-round corrector with a bounded permutation neighborhood. If |U|/|Γ| ≤ ρraw, it maps every word agreeing with Rv outside U to a word agreeing with Rv outside a set U+ determined only by U, with |U+| ≤ |U|/2. Consequently t rounds leave a prescribed uncertainty support of density at most 2−t|U|/|Γ|. The guarantee holds for arbitrary values on U. Different requested-center simulations may use different values there, provided repeated occurrences of a position are consistent within each individual cone. (v) Global recovery. From any word within ρraw symbol distance of a valid word, a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm recovers its exact extended label and raw word. It then recovers the logical bits by systematic coefficient extraction and evaluation on the subgroup. In particular it extracts an End-of-Line answer whenever the recovered label is a nonexceptional endpoint. (vi) Uniform cost and order of choices. The total raw data and listed public descriptions have N poly(ℓN ) bits and are constructible in poly(N) time. Each raw local test, proposed symbol, flag, and one-round corrector has a Boolean circuit of size at most CLcraw on a fixed number of symbols. For each fixed t, correction for t rounds followed by any such raw routine has size at most CtLcraw and at most O(Qt) symbol ports, with uniform construction for that t. The exponents CL, craw are fixed before t and any later port arity. Further fixed additive padding in Cbase has only linear processing cost and does not change these exponents or arities.

candidates.label: Theorem 6.1
candidates.name: Standardized ports and robust decisions
candidates.heading: Theorem 6.1 (Standardized ports and robust decisions).
candidates.statement: For every fixed positive integer exponent allowance callow, there are a cutoff Lport and a uniform family of injective binary encodings, for L ≥ Lport, D : {0, 1}L −→ {0, 1}S0 , S0 = poly(L), with fixed positive relative distance dB, satisfying (i)– (ii) below. The radius νB in (iii) is fixed with this port family; the actual-gadget assertions in that part have the separate later cutoff specified there. (i) Every coordinate of D(s) is a multilinear polynomial in the bits of s over F2, of degree at most 10. Its coefficient list is computable in time polynomial in L. The degree bound is independent of callow. Encoding and exact recovery from a fixed positive relative-error radius are deterministic polynomial-time algorithms. 49 (ii) A perfect-completeness tester makes a bounded number of bit queries and performs bounded Boolean answer processing. Its public randomness has an enumerable polynomial-size rational support and polynomial bit complexity. For every fixed a > 0, there are a fixed θB(a) > 0 and a cutoff LB(a) ≥ Lport, allowed to depend on a, such that for every L ≥ LB(a) rejection below θB(a) implies distance less than a from D({0, 1}L). A word at distance a from an encoding has rejection at most CBa, for a fixed CB. Each fixed-branch query has a bounded-density marginal relative to the uniform distribution on the block. These assertions include arbitrary words and all hypothetical branches. (iii) There is a constant 0 < νB < dB/4 determined with this encoding, before any arity is specified. Subsequently fix an arity bound k, a size factor Cf , and a desired output loss υ > 0. Some inputs may be declared public 0L. There is a uniform generalized subcircuit for this function, with a common count scale G0 = poly(L) for all padded functions under these bounds, at most CgG0 gates, and a set of W designated output wires produced by its gates, where cgG0 ≤ W ≤ CgG0. (6.1) Here cg, Cg > 0 are fixed. Each nonpublic external input is a block of physical reads X = 3x−1, with x ∈ [0, 1], compared to a public common rational threshold ξ ∈ [2/5, 3/5]. Every external comparison occurrence in the complete unfolded subcircuit can be routed separately to an external replica. For each external port position, the total number of these occurrences is at most CoccG0/S0, (6.2) uniformly over ξ, the function, and its public parameters. This counts all hypothetical branches, including unsuccessful and default branches. There are fixed δg, γg, εg > 0 with the following universal soundness property. For any subsequently chosen fixed physical margin ω > 0, use 0 < ε ≤ εg, ε < ω/1000. Suppose at most γgG0 external comparison occurrences fail to have a physical value on the side of ξ specified by the corresponding bit of yj, at gap greater than ω. Repeated occurrences need not have consistent physical values. Then every assignment of the internal nodes in [0, 1] with at most δgG0 failed gates makes all but υW designated wires correct near-bits for f(s1, . . . , sk): at most ε for zero and at least 1 − ε for one. The port construction and νB are independent of k, Cf , υ. The later constants, the gate-count bounds, and the topology bounds may depend on these fixed choices, but not on L, ξ, or the later margin ω. The threshold may appear as a rational gate parameter. Construction and other parameter computations take polynomial time in L and the supplied description lengths, including the bit length of ξ; all parameter lengths are bounded by a polynomial in these quantities. In particular an arbitrarily long externally supplied threshold is charged for its bits.

candidates.label: Proposition 8.5
candidates.name: Smooth tester and distance
candidates.heading: Proposition 8.5 (Smooth tester and distance).
candidates.statement: For each fixed template, the canonical encodings of valid extended labels have constant relative distance. (ii) There is a perfectly complete tester using a bounded number of bit reads and bounded Boolean processing. Its public randomness is uniformly enumerable with polynomial-size support and rational probabilities of polynomial bit length. For every fixed a > 0, there is a fixed θB(a) > 0 such that rejection less than θB(a) implies proximity less than a to some D(s), for all sufficiently large L. candidates.label: Proposition A.1
candidates.name: Full macrograph polynomial representation
candidates.heading: Proposition A.1 (Full macrograph polynomial representation).
candidates.statement: For a normalized End-of-Line instance of encoding length N, one can construct in deterministic polynomial time a cyclic macrograph and its progress-path extension with the following properties. (iii) The tuples have a perfectly complete bounded binary-form algebraic validator with a constant exact gap on genuine degree-at-most-D polynomials. Linear probes are smooth; each unknown product uses two independent full point marginals. Canonical recipes with the same degree and covariance properties are defined on every Boolean logical tape at every specified frame, mode, and progress. An invalid label so represented has the same exact gap. (iv) Mode, empty/full progress, and the critical bits for a proposed edit admit bounded smooth decisions at any fixed reliability. Once the true decision branch is fixed, either proposed canonical tuple has the bounded affine update formulas of (7.46), including its full proof data, whether or not the proposed target is valid. The coefficients are independent of point and row position, and the updates commute with common linear row encodings and ordered-line coefficient encodings. Here the fields and all fixed constants are chosen for this whole construction. No common one-port source or radius-before-arity conclusion is asserted. Target validity is tested after prediction, as in Proposition A.3; it is not presumed by an affine update formula.

candidates.label: Proposition A.2
candidates.name: All ordered products and full logical recovery
candidates.heading: Proposition A.2 (All ordered products and full logical recovery).
candidates.statement: Fix an inner algebraic template, and replace the compatible-pair list by the list of all ordered pairs of point-track types in (8.5). The two positions remain independent even when the types coincide; no line-product blocks are added. 141 Rebalance all blocks by the repetition construction of Section 8.2. This encoding has polynomial length and a uniform polynomial-time construction, and has the following properties. (i) Valid canonical words have constant distance and the perfectly complete smooth tester and proximity guarantee of Proposition 8.5. A structurally canonical word whose label is invalid has rejection probability at least one fixed θinv > 0. (ii) One fixed radius permits arbitrary fixed average accuracy for bounded-density requests, with joint pair density for products, arbitrary public masks and forms, and all-hypothetical-branch smoothness as in Proposition 8.10 and Lemma 8.11. (iii) From a sufficiently small fixed neighborhood of any structurally canonical word, its entire logical tape b = (w, e, (si)i) is recoverable exactly in deterministic polynomial time, whether or not that tape is valid. The constants and the radius may depend on the whole fixed template and its block list. No common one-port layout or radius fixed before arity is asserted for this variant. More generally, the same binary transfer applies to a supplied fixed finite chart template with the field, degree, slot, and polynomial-size bounds used in Section 8, subject to these explicit conditions: its canonical recipes are defined also on invalid logical tapes; its bounded binary-form algebraic validator has perfect completeness and an exact constant gap on genuine degree-in-bound polynomial tuples; its linear probes have bounded point marginals and its products have independent full point marginals; and its order-one grid charts and constant mode/marker tensors separate labels. Full logical recovery requires order-one grid charts for every logical coordinate. This transfer assumes these algebraic properties; it does not assert that the fixed-input path of Section 7 realizes an arbitrary macrograph.

candidates.label: Proposition A.3
candidates.name: Prediction before target validation
candidates.heading: Proposition A.3 (Prediction before target validation).
candidates.statement: Use the unrestricted representation of Proposition A.2. Suppose a valid current label has a prescribed proposal chosen by finitely many decisions which are recoverable, to any fixed reliability, by bounded smooth bit procedures. On a valid current label, once its true decision branch is fixed, suppose the full canonical proposed tuple is a definite structurally canonical tuple, possibly invalid, whose contractions are bounded sums of public terms and old contractions at invertible K-affine target pulls. For each branch these pulls must belong to a fixed bounded public list, independent of the requested outer indices and mask or form values. Masks may select terms from that list and determine their slot pulls and forms. Require bounded slot expansions, coefficients independent of target point and row, compatibility with the common row and line encodings, and publicly computable actual encoded values for public terms. On hypothetical wrong branches only these bounded schedules and smooth defaults are required; a canonical target identity is asserted only when the branch predicates hold. All branch lists, supports, and public computations are to have the uniform polynomial-size bounds of Section 8. From a sufficiently small fixed neighborhood of the current valid word, its proposed word can be predicted to arbitrary fixed average accuracy on bounded-density requests before deciding target validity. That validity can then be decided with arbitrary fixed reliability. If an actual-edge predicate is exactly target validity together with specified public or similarly recoverable guards, this also decides that edge flag. All routines are bounded on every received word and retain the complete hypothetical-tree smoothness bound. No reciprocity of a general proposed graph is inferred from target validity alone.

manuscripts.title: Simulating One-Tape Time in Two-Fifths-Power Space

candidates.heading: Theorem 1.

manuscripts.title: Uniform bounds for planar polynomial limit cycles

candidates.label: Theorem 1.1
candidates.name: Uniform boundedness
candidates.heading: Theorem 1.1 (Uniform boundedness).
candidates.statement: For each integer d ≥ 1, there is a finite nonnegative integer B(d) such that every real planar polynomial vector field of degree at most d has at most B(d) limit cycles in the whole plane.

candidates.label: Theorem 3.2
candidates.name: Separation
candidates.heading: Theorem 3.2 (Separation).
candidates.statement: Suppose the data of Definition 3.1 satisfy its requirements on a saturated flag. If all paired terminal coefficients vanish, the actual function is identically zero on the real flag locus sufficiently far in the regime, locally in ordinary inputs. Otherwise, let λ = (λ1, . . . , λm) be the first nonzero paired exponent. Its coefficients coincide as ordinary analytic germs, say c+ λ = c− λ = cλ, and exp m X i=1 λiZi ! In band j, use its raw packet and normalize by the remaining selected exponents, evaluating all these rates with bj. The coupled normalized determinations have the same leading limit inside their selected contours and through the used bands. With (3.4), their leading estimates extend through the owning outer fringe for any fixed required normalization. An entire zero subtree in band p + 1, passed at such a prefix, has size O(e−cVp ) (3.9) on more vertical level-p collars and on the subsequent portion of that fringe, where its outer determination is in use. All constants and contour choices concern fixed finite labels and requests; none is asserted uniform over the whole packet tree.

candidates.label: Theorem 4.4
candidates.name: Packet calculus
candidates.heading: Theorem 4.4 (Packet calculus).
candidates.statement: Assume the flag estimates of Section 2, the packet separation theorem, and Assumption 4.2. Start with the primitive data and the initial ordinary backgrounds. The following operations can be iterated a finite number of times. 1. Raw finite sums, products, and any fixed independent derivatives have differentiated packet trees with iterated left-finite supports. So does multiplication by any fixed real exponential monomial hγ = exp − X i γiZi ! . 2. Positive expressions admit cleaned zeroth-prefix realizations Kj. Every fixed ordinary derivative is bounded and converges to the corresponding derivative of K0 throughout the usable bands. If a mixed independent derivative has earliest differentiated free index l, then for j ≤ l its value 39 on Kj, multiplied by eCfl(u), tends to zero for every fixed C. Differentiated owning transitions satisfy Kj − Kj+1 = O(e−cℜZj,j ). Real local uniform boundedness of a raw expression implies positivity; its real limit, when specified, identifies K0. 3. A regular analytic operation on finitely many positive expressions, whose limiting tuple belongs to its analytic domain, is positive and has the corresponding differentiated tree. This includes inversion of a unit whose limiting value is nonzero. 4. Let K(S, t, x) be a real square vector of positive expressions on a previous chart. If K0(tc, xc) = 0, det DxK0(tc, xc) ̸= 0, then the actual regular branch x = χ(S, t) near (tc, xc) and every old raw expression pulled back to that branch have differentiated packet trees. The new backgrounds obey Equation (4.2). The ordinary limiting root is analytic. Band realizations are smooth regular sheets, holomorphic in band 1, with controlled jets, differentiated source bounds, safe-column estimates, and differentiated seam bounds. They retain local independence from discarded free inputs. For each fixed finite stack of ordinary implicit charts there is a finite coherence jet order, depending on the stack and fixed angular buffers but independent of subsequent derivative orders and transition budgets. Tests on the same free path with the same complex ordinary target and enough common real jets give the same local sheet. Every finite request can then use a larger working Taylor order and farther or narrower working domains; on overlaps these constructions agree. All assertions for a fixed finite request are uniform on controlled families in the sense of Definition 4.1. All formal operations are performed separately in the two signs, by finite coefficient rules at successive prefixes. They commute with differentiation, regular analytic substitution, and the stated regular implicit solution. Identically zero terminal coefficient germs remain zero under these rules.

candidates.label: Proposition 5.5
candidates.name: Elimination with a deferred floor
candidates.heading: Proposition 5.5 (Elimination with a deferred floor).
candidates.statement: Let F be a real positive scalar field on an active chart with n ordinary inputs. The following statements hold simultaneously. 1. In exact mode, along anchors where F = 0, finitely many regular changes, promotions, and exact ordinary restrictions produce a chart through those anchors on which F has identically zero formal data and hence vanishes on its real regime. All old free inputs survive. 2. If FA is visible relative to a numerical floor, there is a full-dimensional regular chart with an exact hit and F = τU, (5.10) where τ is a nonnegative-order monomial, possibly 1, and U is positive with nonzero exponent- zero value at the limiting hit. All added divisors, widths, and local conditioning costs are power moderate in |FA|. The active ordinary count does not increase. 3. If FA is negligible, active flag additions and their reference records can be chosen without realizing the floor. For every eventual realization r, field tolerance M, finite derivative request k, and record accuracy A, there is a full-dimensional regular chart hitting the input, of active ordinary count at most n, on which |F| ≤ rM . (5.11) Its added divisions and widths are power moderate in r. Its records at the hit differ from the references by O(rA), and their inverse first derivatives in the exogenous inputs, at fixed physical inputs, are O(rA) on a power-sized neighborhood. The third assertion has the following stronger order of quantifiers. For fixed M, r, k, the thickness exponents, forward bounds for the actual map and its record outputs through order at least max(k, 2), inverse-Jacobian powers, and source and physical-image neighborhood exponents can all be fixed before A is requested. Constants and sufficiently far starting points may depend on A. The denominator powers in an individual finite flattened formula may depend on A. Completed active charts remain fixed as A increases; only pending thickness recipes and their finite Taylor replays are refined. The construction also has the following prefix invariant. For the fixed request before choosing A, there is a fixed finite chronological list of coordinate replacements and scaling exponents. Every prefix has the same ordinary limiting regular equations and analytic argument germs throughout the accuracy family. Its maps and records, with the unknown of a subsequent equation still an independent ordinary input, have preassigned finite derivative and source-domain powers; its inverse and image powers are preassigned where an inverse is used. Its monomial divisors belong to powers of a fixed finite list of moderate current monomials and their triangular derivative factors. Only 60 their multiplicities inside the finite formulas can grow with accuracy. Thus the family meets the hypotheses and conclusions of Lemma 5.4 at every pending lift.

candidates.label: Theorem 5.7
candidates.name: Absolute isolated-zero finiteness
candidates.heading: Theorem 5.7 (Absolute isolated-zero finiteness).
candidates.statement: Let a finite real equation system be specified on an open domain with its original strict inequalities and graph ties. Regard all coordinates, including coefficient parameters and auxiliary coordinates, as variables. Suppose every sequence of distinct solutions has a subsequence with one of the following descriptions: 1. the equations extend as ordinary real analytic functions to a neighborhood of its finite limit; or 2. after finitely many regular graph constructions and coordinate charts, it is an anchored saturated flag regime for a library retestable in the sense of Definition 5.6, with at least one old free 65 input recoverable from the original solution tuple. In the second description every equation admits the finite normalizations and positive operations of Theorem 4.4. Then the system has finitely many isolated real solutions in its full domain. The assertion applies separately to every finite system in the following closure whenever these same sequential hypotheses hold: independent derivatives of equations and domain margins; finite sums, products and regular analytic evaluations; inverses on their specified nonzero domains; denom- inator clearing with those domains retained; fixed real specializations; addition of real parameters, multiplier variables, polynomial equations, and regular graph ties, including finite derivative graphs. No uniform bound over infinitely many generated systems, and no assertion after forgetting their original domains, is part of this theorem.

candidates.label: Theorem 6.1
candidates.name: Additive primitive packets
candidates.heading: Theorem 6.1 (Additive primitive packets).
candidates.statement: Under these assumptions, the output maps of (6.5) and (6.6) satisfy the packet conditions of Definition 3.1 and the differentiated primitive conditions of Assumption 4.2. They have no exceptional column loss: every working column is safe. Their only nonholomorphic defects above the first band have simple costs eℜfi and, when q is large, eℜfl , where i, l are the leading indices of Q, q. Each cost is used only while its log formula is retained. The complete terminal coefficient germs, on each lateral determination, are unchanged by inserting unused nodes and by retesting a fixed finite construction on a permitted refinement preserving the old active free nodes, with the same lifted relations and limiting ordinary data. In particular this primitive library is retestable for elimination in the sense of Definition 5.6, with the fixed local lateral determinations.

candidates.label: Theorem 8.1
candidates.name: Mixed passage packets
candidates.heading: Theorem 8.1 (Mixed passage packets).
candidates.statement: Suppose that the primary inputs are affine combinations of flag scales with constant coefficients and bounded analytic parts, and that all large basis nodes in those combinations have dependent logarithms. For an unbalanced limit, put P = max(L, W) and R = min(L, W) on the reference sequence, and include a primary input Caux → ∞ tied there to P/R. Then the outputs of Equations (8.1) and (8.2) satisfy the primitive hypotheses of Assumption 4.2, including fixed independent derivatives, simultaneous safe columns, and refinement invariance of terminal analytic germs. They are retestable for elimination in the sense of Definition 5.6. The amplitude and input smallness is independent of expansion depth. For a family of positive limiting slopes it can also be chosen independently of the slope, provided the ordinary boxes and field bounds are common and every field monomial contains a designated layer whose limiting rate has a common positive lower bound. candidates.heading: Theorem 9.7 (Finite passage templates).
candidates.statement: For each degree bound d, there is a finite collection of scalar identity pieces, coordinate charts and passage rules, and integers Nd, Ed, with the following properties. 1. On the square, every polynomial field of degree at most d has the stated finite globally subanalytic subdivision. Its interior scalar fields are constant-state fields, nozero or simple-root boxes of Equation (9.9), or monomial annuli of Equation (9.6). Their analytic factors have uniform larger neighborhoods and their nonconstant arguments have the prescribed fixed smallness. All changes back to physical coordinates use parameter-only data, positive rational powers, and bounded analytic operations. 2. The further real passage refinements in Section 10 are finite; in particular Lemma 9.5 allows at most one weighted redo at a nonzero generator resonance. 3. Apart from at most Ed periodic orbits containing tangential boundary arcs, every periodic orbit is a cyclic concatenation of at most Nd interior passages and physical graph connectors. There are only finitely many resulting words, including all choices of chart, sign, orientation, and the finitely many endpoint passage rules. The choices and bounds include all coefficient degeneracies.

candidates.label: Theorem 10.1
candidates.name: Terminal reduction
candidates.heading: Theorem 10.1 (Terminal reduction).
candidates.statement: Fix the finite preparation data, exponent lists, and geometric tolerances of Theorem 9.7. After finitely many further real subanalytic subdivisions, every terminal 128 passage is represented by one scalar transfer equation and regular, locally unique argument graphs. The transfer is an ordinary analytic transfer, an additive transfer of Theorem 6.1, a one-rate transfer of Theorem 7.1, or a mixed transfer of Theorem 8.1. More precisely, the following statements hold. 1. These are actual real ODE transfers on open independent-argument domains. The domains have finite lists of strict clock, sign, divisor, analytic-box, amplitude, and state-room margins. A bounded limit at which these margins remain positive is an analytic point of the transfer family. At bounded-clock corners, adding the indicated bounded ratios gives analytic normalized transfers also at zero clock limits, with state room. 2. At fixed physical parameters, on the graph of the argument ties near an actual passage, the equation is the physical mismatch in regular transverse coordinates. This identity holds for independently proposed nearby endpoints, before imposing the transfer equation. 3. For an arbitrary sequence of arguments and any fixed finite collection of independent-argument derivatives, the transfers and those derivatives reduce to the preceding packet primitives and bounded analytic operations. This assertion includes sequences on which any of the imposed strict margins tend to zero; it does not assume the positive-margin condition in the first assertion. When all enlarged normalized arguments stay bounded, the kernel factors have analytic extensions with state room after the finite graph additions, and algebraic divisors can be cleared. If an added argument diverges, its recoverable coordinate is included in the packet test. The reduction may introduce bounded ratios and a fixed finite internal subdivision chosen for that sequence. The old derivatives are obtained by the chain rule for exact transfer identities. The internal state and finite jet graphs are locally unique and preserve isolated solutions. The coefficient determinations are those fixed by the primitive theorems and are preserved under their allowed retests. The number of geometric passage types and boundary crossings is finite. Internal subdivisions in the last assertion do not enter that number. Geometric smallness is fixed before a limiting slope or any asymptotic or derivative request is selected.

manuscripts.title: Uniform Permanence in Weakly Reversible Mass-Action Systems

candidates.label: Theorem 1.1
candidates.heading: Theorem 1.1.
candidates.statement: Let C ⊂ Zd ≥0 be finite, let R ⊂ C × C be weakly reversible, and fix positive rate constants in (1.1). For every positive stoichiometric class P there is a nonempty compact convex set KP ⊂ P with the following properties. Every initial point x0 ∈ P gives a unique global positive solution, and there is a finite T(x0) ≥ 0 such that x(t) ∈ KP (t ≥ T(x0 )). Moreover, KP is forward invariant. In particular, there is εP ∈ (0, 1), depending only on the network, the fixed rates, and P, such that every such solution satisfies εP ≤ xi(t) ≤ ε−1 P (1 ≤ i ≤ d, t ≥ T(x0 )). (1.2)
